verification: Reproduced the original evidence by executing the shipped module: normalizeRepeatHistory({'ubereats.com':[now-2y, now-1.5y]}) with no options still returns both timestamps, which is the call the report ran. The RUNTIME path no longer does that — readSettings passes {now, windowMinutes} and returns {}, recordContinue prunes on write, and refreshBlockingState writes the pruned map back through pruneStoredRepeatHistory. Proved on disk in real Chrome (149.0.7827.55) against the built package rather than in Node: seeded chrome.storage.local with rows 1, 2 and 3 years old plus one fresh row, ran a refresh, then read chrome.storage.local back and saw only {'doordash.com':[<fresh>]} — every years-old row was gone from disk. Two gaps the report did not name were still open and are now fixed: (1) switching repeat friction OFF left the whole brand-keyed relapse diary frozen on disk forever, because nothing cleared a map whose only reader had been turned off — pruneStoredRepeatHistory now writes {} in that case and grantPass writes nothing back; (2) the keys that decide retention were not refresh keys, so a change to them was not re-evaluated until the next browser restart — repeatFrictionEnabled is now in REFRESH_KEYS. The third sub-claim, the missing docs row, is closed by docs/STORAGE.md line 30 plus a rewritten Repeat-access history section; the fourth, no targeted delete, is closed by settings.js BLOCKING_KEYS which now names repeatHistory; the fifth, the stale 'short-lived' comment in backup.js, is now true. Separately, repeatWindowMinutes turned out to be written by NOTHING in the product — no control, no friction preset, no install seed — so retention could only ever be the default while the key was carried in every backup and named by a reset button; it is now a documented constant and a stored value is ignored outright.
evidenceAfter: on-disk repeatHistory after a refresh with 1/2/3-year-old rows seeded: {"doordash.com":[1786287604854]} — only the fresh row survived

verification: Reproduced by running the shipped redactReportSubject over the exact four inputs in the report. All three that leaked now reduce to a bare host: 'http://192.168.1.50/admin?token=SECRET123' -> '192.168.1.50', 'https://localhost:3000/checkout?card=4111111111111111' -> 'localhost', 'https://ubereats.com./store?q=late+night' -> 'ubereats.com', and 'http://[2001:db8::1]/order?session=abc' -> '2001:db8::1'. The dotted-alpha regex gate that fell through to cleanText(text,120) on the raw string is gone; an input that parses as a URL never reaches the raw-text fallback, which is reserved for free text like 'the checkout page' (still passed through, still capped at 120). The on-screen promise at settings.html reportPrivacyNote is therefore true for every host shape, not only the common one.

Attacked empirically in Chrome 149 from a genuinely hostile page served over http://evil.example/ with every hostname mapped to a local observer, not by handing a fake sender to a Node harness. Three routes were tried. (1) Direct messaging: chrome.runtime is not exposed to a web page at all — the manifest declares no externally_connectable, so a website cannot reach the worker by any message. (2) Hidden iframes: 12 loads of chrome-extension://<id>/warning.html?site=delivery-doordash-com, including nested depth-2 frames, moved nothing — stats.totals.interruptions stayed 2 and blockedByDomain, blockedByCategory and blockedByCountry were byte-identical before and after. That is the frameId!==0 guard holding in a real browser. (3) The route the report and the guard both missed, which DID reproduce: a website can simply navigate the tab to that URL, which is a top-level document on our own origin with frameId 0. Four such navigations moved interruptions from 2 to 6 and wrote doordash.com into blockedByDomain. Fixed by giving the worker's declarativeNetRequest redirect URL a random 128-bit token (chrome.storage.session, adopted from the persisted rules on a cold browser session so a restart cannot lose a real interruption) and refusing any durable-state message from a block page whose own URL does not carry the current token. A website can construct every other part of that URL; it can read neither the dynamic rules nor session storage. Re-ran the same four forced navigations against the fixed package: interruptions stayed 2 and the brand breakdown did not move. Preview URLs stay exempt and are now proven to record nothing, with the preview flag read from the sender's URL instead of trusted from the message body, so a page can no longer claim to be recording for real or claim not to be.
evidenceAfter: before the fix: 4 top-level navigations to warning.html took interruptions 2 -> 6; after: 4 identical navigations left interruptions at 2 and blockedByDomain unchanged

verification: Same empirical attack as F034, aimed at the specific claim: a 1x1 hidden iframe of warning.html in a loop. Ran 8 hidden iframes plus 4 nested (evil page -> same-origin frame -> block page, so frameId is two levels deep) against the built package in Chrome 149, waited for all 12 loads to complete, and compared storage before and after: every counter in stats.totals unchanged, blockedByDomain / blockedByCategory / blockedByCountry unchanged, no pass created. The worker refuses on sender.frameId !== 0 because the DNR rule is main_frame-only, so a framed sender is never a real block page. Went further than the finding asked in two ways. Read-only handlers are now refused from a framed surface too — getBlockState, getBlockContext and getDiagnostics return the user's diet, allergens, pantry and their own written-out recipes, and nothing FitShield ships runs in a frame. And the loud sibling of this attack, a top-level navigation, is closed by the redirect token (see F034). The finding's suggested use_dynamic_url was evaluated and rejected: dynamic rules persist across browser restarts while the dynamic URL rotates per session, so the persisted redirect target would break; the token achieves the same unguessability without that failure mode. frame-ancestors 'none' was also measured and rejected — Chrome accepts it in extension_pages and does not apply it to a web_accessible_resource loaded by a website, so shipping it would read as protection while providing none.
evidenceAfter: 12 framed block-page loads (8 direct + 4 nested/depth-2): interruptions stayed 2, blockedByDomain unchanged, 0 passes

verification: Reproduced the reporting path end to end rather than reading it. backup.js now throws errors carrying both an English sentence and an i18nKey plus substitutions; ran all five rejection paths through the shipped module and each returned a distinct key: empty file -> backupErrorEmptyFile, 3 MB file -> backupErrorTooLarge with subs ['3072','2048'], malformed JSON -> backupErrorInvalidJson, schema 99 -> backupErrorNewerFormat with subs ['99'], and a file with no FitShield keys -> backupErrorNoSettings. The UI no longer discards them: settings.js backupErrorMessage() localizes error.i18nKey with its substitutions, falls back to the English sentence backup.js wrote for a person, and only reaches the generic importErrorNotice for an error from somewhere else entirely; welcome.js does the same. The specific harm the finding named — telling a user that a backup written by a NEWER FitShield 'isn't a valid FitShield backup', which invites them to delete their only copy — now reads 'That backup was written by a newer version of FitShield (format 99). Update FitShield, then import it.' A separate wrong message was fixed alongside it: a failure to WRITE an export reported the import error, which is nonsense when no file exists yet.
evidenceAfter: empty -> backupErrorEmptyFile; 3MB -> backupErrorTooLarge subs ["3072","2048"]; bad JSON -> backupErrorInvalidJson; schema 99 -> backupErrorNewerFormat subs ["99"]; no known keys -> backupErrorNoSettings

verification: Traced the import path in settings.js as it stands and confirmed the shape the finding asked for exists and is ordered correctly: the file is parsed and normalized FIRST (pure, touching no storage), then confirmAction() is awaited with a message that names what will be overwritten and what will be cleared — the active temporary pass and any unanswered 'did you make it?' prompt, which are exactly the two the finding said nothing warned about — and only then is applyImport() called. Declining leaves storage untouched and reports 'Import cancelled. Nothing was changed.' The separation is structural, not incidental: backup.js exposes parseBackup/normalizeImported and applyImport as distinct entry points precisely so a caller can validate, say what will happen, wait for a yes, and only then write, and test/backup.test.js drives a rejected file through the pure half and asserts chrome.storage.local.remove and .set are never called. Exercised the whole flow in real Chrome as part of the session acceptance: opened Settings, ran an export, then ran sixteen hostile files through parseBackup/normalizeImported in the page, and blocking was still armed with 2575 rules and www.doordash.com still redirected afterwards.
evidenceAfter: settings.js import path: normalizeImported(parseBackup(text)) -> confirmAction(confirmImportBackup, [count]) -> applyImport(settings); a declined confirm writes nothing and reports importCancelledNotice

verification: Reproduced the exact fixture from the report — a backup carrying three custom alternatives all with id 'dup' — through the shipped import path, and the ids that come out are now ['dup','custom-mslwn1zm-1','custom-mslwn1zm-2']. normalizeCustomAlternatives still preserves the id an entry arrived with, as it must; the deduplication is in backup.js withUniqueIds, which runs on import and re-issues a fresh id to any collision, checking each candidate against both the ids already kept AND every id the file carried so a replacement cannot collide with an entry further down the list. A colliding entry is re-issued rather than dropped because it is the user's own content and losing it would be the worse failure. The harm the finding named — deleting one recipe silently deleting every entry sharing its id, and editing one collapsing them all — is gone because the ids preferences.js filters on are now distinct. Also asserted as a property across sixteen fuzzed hostile backups: every accepted file yields a customAlternatives list whose ids are unique.
evidenceAfter: three entries all id 'dup' import as ["dup","custom-mslwn1zm-1","custom-mslwn1zm-2"]

verification: Checked the built artifacts rather than the build script. dist/chrome/data contains only recipes.json — data/android and data/generated are absent from both dist/chrome and dist/firefox. Enumerated the local file headers of dist/FitShield-0.55-chrome.zip directly and found 116 entries, none matching /android|generated/, against the 120 entries and four Android payload files the report enumerated; the zip is 739,530 bytes against the ~5.3 MB staged size the report measured. What changed: build.js now separates the Android-only dataset prefixes from the shared DIRS list (build.ANDROID_ONLY_PREFIXES) and asserts their absence while staging (build.assertNoAndroidPayload), landed in commit ef8004d 'popup, block page, packaging: close ten assigned findings; drop 17% of both packages'. The datasets still exist canonically under data/ for the Android build, which the same test asserts.
evidenceAfter: dist/FitShield-0.55-chrome.zip: 116 local entries, 0 matching android|generated, 739530 bytes; dist/chrome/data contains only recipes.json

verification: Reproduced the count on the exact case the report named and found it still wrong, for a second reason. Excluding the schema marker had been done, but a pre-0.55 file carrying six settings (blockedVisits, recipesChosen, enabled, timerSeconds, theme, uiLanguage) still reported seven, because the migration ALSO adds a derived `stats` key translated from the very blockedVisits/recipesChosen already being counted — so the notice double-counted the legacy counters. restoredCount now reports the number of settings the FILE carried, recorded inside normalizeImported while the file is still in view, minus the schema marker whether or not the file carried one. It travels on a Symbol-keyed property, which Object.keys, JSON.stringify and chrome.storage.local.set all step over, so it can never be mistaken for data or written to storage. Re-ran both cases: the six-setting legacy file now reports 6 (was 7), and a modern six-key file still reports 6. A file that explicitly carries schemaVersion alongside one real setting reports 1.
evidenceAfter: pre-0.55 file carrying 6 settings: restoredCount 7 -> 6; modern 6-key file: 6; {schemaVersion, enabled}: 1
